steps: A force may change the speed of an object. It may make a stationary object move, or a moving object stop.
A force may change the direction of motion of an object.
A force may change both the speed and direction of motion of an object.
items.finalAnswer: A force can change an object’s speed, direction, or both.

steps: Examples of contact forces are:
1. Frictional force
2. Tension force
3. Normal force
4. Air resistance
5. Spring force
items.finalAnswer: Frictional, tension, normal, air-resistance and spring forces are examples of contact forces.

steps: According to Newton’s first law, an object continues moving with constant velocity unless acted upon by an external force.
In free space, if no external force acts on the object, it will continue moving with that velocity indefinitely.
items.finalAnswer: The object will continue to move with constant velocity indefinitely, as long as no external force acts on it.

steps: The product of a force and the time for which it acts is called the impulse of the force.
Impulse = Force × Time interval
It is equal to the change in momentum of the object: I = FΔt = Δp.
items.finalAnswer: Impulse is the product of a force and the time interval for which it acts, and equals the change in momentum.

steps: Newton’s first law cannot be proved on the Earth because a completely frictionless surface cannot be obtained.
A moving object on the Earth experiences friction and air resistance, which oppose its motion and eventually stop it.
items.finalAnswer: It cannot be proved on Earth because friction and air resistance act on moving objects.

steps: When the car accelerates forward, the part of your body in contact with the seat moves forward with the car.
Due to inertia, the rest of your body tends to remain in its initial state of rest.
Therefore, you appear to be pushed backward into the seat.
items.finalAnswer: Due to inertia, your body tends to remain at rest as the car accelerates forward, so you appear to be pushed back.

steps: Several forces may act on an object at the same time.
The resultant of all the forces acting on an object is called the net force.
Balanced forces cancel one another and do not produce acceleration; only an unbalanced (net) force produces acceleration.
Therefore, Newton’s second law relates acceleration to the net force acting on an object.
items.finalAnswer: Newton’s second law uses net force because only the resultant, unbalanced force produces acceleration.

steps: Place a block on a table and pull it horizontally with a spring balance. Note the force required to keep it moving; this measures sliding friction.
Now place rollers (cylindrical rods) between the block and the table and pull the block with the spring balance again.
The spring-balance reading is smaller when the block rolls on the rollers than when it slides on the table.
Therefore, rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
items.finalAnswer: A smaller spring-balance reading when the block rolls on rollers shows that rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
